analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare beneficiaries buy prescription drugs at the discounted prices the federal government already pays.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors, sent to two House committees and their health subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government buys prescription drugs for its own use through contracts listed on the Federal Supply Schedule, at prices well below what consumers pay at the pharmacy. This one-sentence bill would have let anyone on Medicare — roughly 40 million older and disabled Americans at the time — buy their prescriptions at those same discounted prices. It went to two House committees, then to their health subcommittees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — older and disabled Americans — would pay substantially less out of pocket for prescriptions, because the Federal Supply Schedule prices the government already negotiates for its own purchases are far below retail. Taxpayers could also benefit indirectly if government health programs bought drugs cheaper.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older and disabled Americans on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: It made every person eligible for Medicare Part A or enrolled in Part B eligible to buy prescription drugs at the Federal Supply Schedule prices — the prices the federal government already pays under its own purchasing contracts.
The bill overrides any conflicting law ('notwithstanding any other provision of law'), so the price right would apply automatically without new program bureaucracy.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug manufacturers, whose revenue would drop if tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries bought at federal contract prices instead of retail. Retail pharmacies might also see margins squeezed on drug sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill was a single sentence with no implementation mechanism: the Federal Supply Schedule is a catalog of prices the government negotiates for its own purchases, and the bill said nothing about how pharmacies or beneficiaries would actually obtain drugs at those prices, who would administer the program, or how disputes with manufacturers would be handled.

Requiring manufacturers to sell to roughly 40 million Medicare beneficiaries at federal contract prices amounts to government price-setting on a large share of the drug market. The industry's argument is that this would reduce revenue available for research into new medicines; how much innovation would actually suffer is disputed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been substantial: retirees today spend heavily out of pocket on prescription drugs, and federal contract prices are far below retail. The main cost falls on drug makers, whose revenue on sales to seniors would have dropped; their good-faith argument is that lower prices mean less money for developing new drugs, though that tradeoff is contested. The bigger flaw is design, not principle: the bill was one sentence with no machinery — no card, no pharmacy rules, no enforcement — to actually connect beneficiaries to those prices, so even its supporters would have had to rewrite it before it could work. As written, the idea was sound but the bill was skeletal.

outcome.mechanism: It went to two House committees and never came out — no hearing, no vote, nothing — and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced the bill on February 5, 2003; no other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees on the day it was introduced, then passed to each committee's Subcommittee on Health within the following week.
No further action was ever taken; the bill sat in subcommittee for the rest of the 108th Congress and expired when it ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers, who kept charging retail and private-plan prices to Medicare beneficiaries; Congress instead created the Medicare Part D drug benefit in 2003 with an explicit provision barring the government from negotiating drug prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, whose pricing stayed untouched

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend federal supply schedule drug prices to Medicare beneficiaries.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair Billy Tauzin, R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out or held a hearing; it died in its health subcommittee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.role: Second committee of referral (has jurisdiction over Medicare)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took action on it.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Fought against government price-setting during the 2003 Medicare drug-benefit debate, which produced the Part D law containing a provision barring the government from negotiating drug prices.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the sponsor was a Democrat, no members of either party signed on as cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled committees took no action.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to sell to every Medicare beneficiary at Federal Supply Schedule prices — the discounted prices the government negotiates for its own purchases — replacing higher retail and private-insurer prices on a huge share of their market. In the same Congress, the drug benefit that did pass (Medicare Part D) was designed to keep the government out of price negotiation, so manufacturers ended the session with their pricing power intact.

Pharmacies would have filled prescriptions at lower federal-schedule prices, compressing their margins, though the bill's one-sentence design gave no guidance on how they would be reimbursed or participate.
